hook: El Libertador, who freed six South American countries from Spanish rule.

pages.x: Simón Bolívar was born in 1783 in Caracas, Venezuela, into one of the richest families in Spanish America. By nine he had lost both parents. His tutor, Simón Rodríguez, filled his head with the ideas of Rousseau.

At 18 he married in Spain, but his young wife died of yellow fever eight months later. He never married again. In 1805, on a hill in Rome, he swore he would not rest until he had freed his country from Spain.

Venezuela declared independence in 1811, but the Spanish crushed the new republic twice. Bolívar fled to Jamaica, where in 1815 he wrote his Jamaica Letter, dreaming of a free and united South America.
In 1819 he led his army across flooded plains and over the freezing passes of the Andes, where many men died of cold. Then he surprised the Spanish at Boyacá and freed what is now Colombia.
He founded Gran Colombia, a great republic of today's Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama, and became its president. His victory at Carabobo in 1821 freed Venezuela.
He drove the Spanish from Peru, and in 1824 his general Sucre won the last great battle, at Ayacucho. The new country of Upper Peru was named Bolivia in his honour.
In 1828 assassins burst into his palace in Bogotá. His partner, Manuela Sáenz, held them off while he escaped through a window. He called her "the liberator of the Liberator".
His great republic broke apart in quarrels. Sick and disappointed, he gave up power in 1830 and died near Santa Marta at 47. "Those who have served the revolution," he wrote, "have ploughed the sea."
Bolívar freed six countries from Spanish rule. He is called El Libertador, and a country, a currency and countless squares are named after him.
pts: Freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and Panama
